title: Service Priority Hedging and Fallbacks — Runbook and Playbook
author: Maya Patel
summary: This runbook defines cross-service priority hedging patterns and concrete fallback modes to preserve SLOs during capacity constraints or partial degradations. It targets SREs and service owners and provides step-by-step triage, automated and manual mitigation actions, telemetry queries, and post-incident review guidance.
audience: SRE oncall, service owners, platform engineering, incident commanders
content:
Overview

This playbook describes how Redwood SREs should apply priority-based hedging and structured fallbacks when one or more services approach or exceed error-budget, latency SLOs, or when capacity shortfalls are detected. The approach combines:
- pre-declared service priority classes and weightings (P0, P1, P2)
- deterministic mitigation actions (rate-limits, degraded-model routing, cache-first responses)
- progressive and reversible steps mapped to telemetry triggers
- communication and ownership steps to avoid accidental over-attenuation

Goals
- Protect customer-facing SLOs for high-priority services while maximizing overall system throughput.
- Make mitigation actions predictable, reversible, and minimally disruptive.
- Ensure all actions are observable and recorded for post-incident analysis.

Definitions and scope
- Hedging: intentional redistribution of capacity/priority away from lower-priority traffic toward higher-priority traffic.
- Fallback: deterministic degraded behavior that returns a lower-cost or cached response rather than a full-quality response.
- Scope: all runtime model-serving, routing, and API-gateway components managed by Redwood. Private-deploy customers may adopt patterns but require separate runbooks.

Priority classes (example mapping)
- P0 (Critical): Customer-facing production APIs with contractual SLAs (e.g., inference endpoints for paying customers).
- P1 (Important): High-volume non-SLA endpoints (internal features, dev-critical).
- P2 (Best-effort): Batch workloads, background indexing, low-tier tenants.

Ownership matrix
- Service owner: defines the priority class for their service and approves fallbacks.
- SRE oncall: executes hedging playbook during incidents and communicates actions.
- Platform infra: implements gated autopilot behaviors (autoscaler, backpressure circuits).

Configuration table (examples)
| Priority | Max allowed concurrent qps | Preferred fallback | Max allowed fallback rate | Typical mitigation order |
| P0 | preserve 100% until P0 error-budget 85% | degraded-model (shorter context) | 0% | 1: scale, 2: route, 3: model-variant |
| P1 | reduce by 30% when cluster >80% CPU | cache-first responses | 10% | 1: limit bursts, 2: partial-cache, 3: deprioritize |
| P2 | pause or shed at 50% cluster CPU | queue-for-later / 503-with-retry-after | 100% | 1: shed, 2: backoff, 3: reroute to cheaper region |

Runbook: triage and immediate actions (ordered)
1) Detect & confirm:
   a) Observe SLO dashboards: 5-minute error-rate and p95 latency crossing thresholds.
   b) Confirm correlated signals: GPU utilization >85%, queue depth rising, autoscaler failing to add nodes.
   c) Validate scope: single region, single model, or global incident.
2) Classify impact by priority class: answer which services are P0/P1/P2 and approximate traffic share. Use the service-priority registry.
3) Execute fast mitigations (10-minute goal):
   a) Pause non-essential batch jobs and orchestration (P2). CLI: kubectl scale --replicas=0 deploy/batch-worker --namespace=batch || platform-scale pause batch-workers
   b) Enable cache-first routing: flip feature flag platform.routing.cache_first=true (requires owner approval for P1 if non-automated).
   c) Apply client-facing throttles to P1/P2 via API-gateway rate limits: curl -XPOST https://gateway.internal/api/rate-limits -d '{"target":"p1","limit":2000}'
4) Escalate to platform if hardware capacity appears degraded: open paging channel with platform oncall and include snapshot of Prometheus graphs and relevant traces.
5) If mitigations insufficient after 15 minutes, progress to fallback variants (see mitigation table) and consider cross-region failover for P0 only.

Metrics and alert mappings (examples)
- Primary SLO signals: p95 latency, 5m error rate, availability 1m window.
- Secondary: GPU utilization, queue length, KV cache hit-rate.
- Example thresholds and alerts:
  - Alert: model-serving:p95_latency > 2.5s for 5m AND error_rate > 0.5% => fire "hedge-consider"
  - Alert: cluster:gpu_utilization > 85% for 10m => fire "capacity-pressure"
  - Alert: cache:hit_rate < 40% with rising traffic => fire "cache-starve"

Telemetry queries (PromQL examples)
- P95 latency (model-serving):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le,service))
- Error rate (5m):
  sum(rate(request_errors_total[5m])) by (service) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) by (service)
- GPU utilization (5m):
  avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_utilization_percent[5m])

Mitigation action matrix (short form)
1) Soft hedges (automatic, reversible):
   - Autoscaler policy: prefer adding cheaper batch nodes but prioritize scheduling P0 pods.
   - Dynamic queue prioritization: pop P0 requests from KV-cache first.
2) Hard hedges (manual or high-confidence automation):
   - Apply rate limits to P1/P2, route to degraded-model variants, or enforce 503s with Retry-After for P2.
3) Fallbacks (quality tradeoff):
   - Degraded-model: switch to a shorter-context model variant or more heavily quantized model. Expected latency drop 20–40% and quality reduction (measure via regression tests).
   - Cache-first: return cached or recently generated embeddings/text with clearly marked response metadata.
   - Synthetic short answer: generate a template short response when model generation is too expensive (for specific product flows only).

Capacity mitigation table (action mapping)
| Trigger | P0 action | P1 action | P2 action | Notes |
| cluster gpu>85% | scale up reserved nodes, cross-region failover if available | reduce concurrency by 30% | pause non-essential batches | P0 must be preserved when error-budget >15% |
| error_budget_consumed >50% | route P0 to fallback-model variant, notify owners | enable cache-first | increase backoff and retries | owners must sign off on long-term routing changes |

Rollback and verification steps
1) Rollback order: reverse mitigation actions in the opposite order they were applied. Prefer automatic rollback when primary telemetry settles below thresholds for two consecutive 5-minute windows.
2) Verify: confirm p95 and error-rate return to acceptable ranges, check cache hit-rate and request success codes.
3) Communicate: update incident channel with Recovered state and list all actions taken including flags flipped and manifests changed.

Operational tooling and automated runbooks
- Feature flags: use platform/flags-service with audit log. Example: ffctl set fallback-mode model-short-context --env prod --scope service:translate
- Autoscaler knobs: ensure autoscaler exposes prioritization weights. Example HPA override: kubectl patch hpa model-server -p '{"spec":{"behavior":{"scaleDown":{"policies":[{"type":"Percent","value":20,"periodSeconds":60}]}}}}'
- Backpressure circuits: toggle at gateway: curl -XPOST https://gateway.internal/toggle-backpressure -d '{"mode":"priority-hedge"}'

Communication and post-action review
1) Incident comms: SRE oncall must post a short summary within 30 minutes listing impact, priority classes affected, immediate mitigations, and expected next steps.
2) Post-incident review: service owner + SRE must run a 72-hour follow-up to review root causes, effectiveness of hedging, regression in quality, and update the service-priority registry if needed.
3) Data capture: export PromQL snapshots, sample traces, feature flag toggles, and CLI command history into the incident folder.

Runbook maintenance and cadence
- Quarterly review: SRE and service owners to review fallback modes, model-variant quality regressions, and update permissible fallback lists.
- After any hedging event: mandatory owner-approved retro within 7 days.

Appendix: example incident timeline (condensed)
- T+0m: Alert fires: p95 > 2.8s and GPU util > 90%
- T+5m: SRE confirms impact and pauses P2 batch jobs; cache-first routing enabled for P1
- T+12m: Autoscaler added nodes but throughput still constrained; route P0 to degraded-model variant
- T+40m: Telemetry stabilizes, begin staged rollback of P1 throttles
- T+60m: All SLOs back within thresholds; document event and schedule retro
runbook_steps: 1) Detect & confirm signals; 2) Classify services by priority; 3) Execute fast mitigations (pause batch, enable cache-first, apply throttles); 4) Escalate to platform for hardware; 5) Progress to fallback variants if needed
metrics_and_alerts: Primary signals: p95 latency, 5m error rate, availability (1m); Secondary: GPU util, queue depth, cache hit-rate; Example alerts: model-serving:p95>2.5s & error_rate>0.5% => hedge-consider; cluster:gpu_util>85% for 10m => capacity-pressure
telemetry_queries: P95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le,service)); Error rate: sum(rate(request_errors_total[5m])) by (service) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) by (service); GPU util: avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_utilization_percent[5m])
ownership_and_comm: Service owner declares priority and fallback approval; SRE oncall executes hedging; platform infra responsible for autoscaler and node provisioning. Incident comms posted within 30 minutes and 72-hour follow-up by owners and SRE.
post_action_and_review: Capture logs, PromQL snapshots, traces, flags, and CLI history. Schedule retro within 7 days. Quarterly review for fallback quality and allowable fallbacks.
